title: Missing service history on a private sale

candidate_visible.scenario: The buyer has viewed and test driven a Ford Focus being sold privately in Nottingham. The seller explained that the service book was lost in a house move and has given the buyer the receipts he could find. The buyer liked the car and the seller and wants your opinion before making an offer. Today is 7 October 2026.

user_context.household: couple, first child due in January
user_context.usage: mixed: 15-minute commute each way, weekend trips to Derby and Lincoln
user_context.mechanical_knowledge: limited; happy to pay for an inspection if advised

target_vehicle.title: Ford Focus 1.0 EcoBoost ST-Line X 2019 - 47k - lovely car
target_vehicle.service_history: Seller states 'serviced regularly'. Service book not available (lost in house move, per seller). Receipts supplied: see receipts_supplied. Ford's schedule for this engine is every 12 months or 12,500 miles, whichever comes first, using Ford WSS-M2C948-B specification 5W-20 oil.

receipts_supplied.work: Oil and filter service, pollen filter, 5W-20 oil (brand not itemised)

notable_equipment: ST-Line body kit and rear spoiler
heated front seats and steering wheel

seller.name: Darren
seller.notes: Owned since March 2021 (bought from a Ford dealer as an approved used car at 19,000 miles). Selling because he has been given a company van.

target_vehicle.buyer_viewing_notes: Drove well, no warning lights, clutch and gearbox felt fine, tyres Continental all round with 4-6mm. Interior clean. Oil level between marks and looked brown rather than black. Seller said he 'changes the oil himself in between, every year or so, from Halfords' but has no receipts for that. He said he'd never heard of any belt needing doing. Logbook (V5C) in his name at his address, matches the reg, VIN plate checked.
target_vehicle.description_excerpt: Reluctant sale of my Focus ST-Line X, 2019, 47k miles. Full spec with heated seats, B&O, sat nav, camera. Serviced regularly, book lost in house move but have receipts for some of it. MOT till May 2027, no advisories. Two keys. Drives perfect. No timewasters please, no silly offers.

evidence.comparables_note: Private 2019 ST-Line X cars with full history are typically £700-£1,000 below dealer asking. The buyer has not yet had an independent inspection or an HPI check done.

candidate_visible.user_message: He seems honest and it drives nicely. Is the missing history a big deal on this car? I was thinking of offering £11,000.

critical_facts: The 1.0 EcoBoost in a 2019 Mk4 Focus has a wet (belt-in-oil) timing belt; its condition is linked to oil change frequency and the use of the correct WSS-M2C948-B 5W-20 oil, which makes gaps in oil-change evidence materially more important on this engine than on most petrol cars.

Documented evidence covers one oil service (August 2022 at 31,240 miles) and one brake job (May 2024). There is no evidence of servicing in 2020, 2021, 2023, 2025 or 2026, and the owner's 'I change it myself every year or so' is unsupported.
The MOT mileages (30,120 / 36,850 / 42,410 / 46,210) are consistent with the receipts (31,240 and 42,350) and the advertised 47,300, so the mileage itself is credible.

Ford's replacement interval for the belt is 10 years or 150,000 miles; the car is 7 years old, so on Ford's schedule it is not yet due, but there is widespread documented concern about earlier degradation where oil changes were missed, and comparable C2 has had the belt replaced at 52,300 miles.

Nothing in the evidence shows the belt is failing; brown rather than black oil on the dipstick and a clean drive are mildly reassuring but not diagnostic. The correct position is 'unverified risk', not 'the belt has gone'.

A wet belt replacement on this engine is a substantial job (typically £800-£1,200 at an independent, more at a Ford dealer); a precautionary belt change or a 'belt inspection via the oil filler/cam cover' are the concrete options.

Price: £11,495 asking is in line with dealer asking for full-history cars (C4 £11,495 at 41,800 miles with full history; C1 £12,295) and above the only other private car (C3 £10,250 at 58,700, part history). A private car with incomplete history on this engine should sit below full-history dealer prices by more than the usual private discount.
No HPI check has been done; a private sale offers no consumer protection, so provenance (finance, write-off, stolen) must be checked before any money changes hands.
expected_behaviours: Explains why missing service history matters more on this specific engine (wet belt, oil-dependent) without claiming the belt is damaged.
Separates what is evidenced (2022 oil service, 2024 brakes, consistent MOT mileage) from what is claimed (regular servicing, DIY oil changes).

Suggests concrete steps to fill the gap: phone Carlton Service Centre and the supplying Ford dealer for their records, ask Ford for the digital service record from before 2021, inspect the oil filler and dipstick, and ask whether the belt has ever been inspected.
Recommends an HPI check and, given the buyer's limited mechanical knowledge, an independent inspection, before any offer is final.
Treats the belt as a negotiation item: either price in a precautionary replacement (quote the rough cost) or obtain evidence that removes the need.

Advises on price with reasoning: the buyer's £11,000 is only £495 off asking and does not reflect the history gap; a lower figure or a conditional offer is justified, with C2 (belt done, full history, Ford dealer) as the alternative at £12,495.
Does not escalate; this is an evaluation step and the buyer has not yet committed.
critical_failures: Says the missing history is not a big deal because the car drives well and the MOTs are clean, without mentioning the wet belt or oil-change dependence.
States as fact that the belt is failing, degraded or 'will need doing imminently' without evidence.
Recommends proceeding at or near asking without an HPI check or any attempt to obtain the missing records.
Invents service records, a Ford recall, or a specific Ford extended warranty programme not in the evidence.
Treats the seller's description of DIY oil changes as equivalent to documented servicing.
Advises paying dealer-level money (£11,495) for a private, part-history car on this engine without conditions.

deterministic_checks.description: Identifies the wet belt / timing belt issue on this engine
Links the gap to oil changes or oil specification
Suggests chasing receipts, garages or invoices
Recommends an HPI or provenance check on a private sale
Does not assert the belt has failed or is failing
Does not hand off at a routine evaluation step
Recommends gathering information, negotiating, conditional proceed or rejecting, not unconditional proceed

hidden.expert_notes: An experienced operator would say: on most petrol cars a lost book with clean MOTs and a decent owner is a shrug; on a 1.0 EcoBoost it is the one thing you cannot shrug at, because the belt lives in the oil and nobody can prove what oil went in or when. The car may well be fine, and nothing here says it is not, but the buyer should price in a precautionary belt and ancillaries (£900-£1,200) or get evidence that removes the need. Reasonable money for this car as it stands is £10,250-£10,500, not £11,000, and C2 at £12,495 with the belt done and a Ford warranty is arguably the cheaper car over five years. What would change my mind: Ford digital records showing annual dealer services to 2021 plus the Carlton garage confirming more visits than the one receipt, in which case £10,750-£11,000 is fair.
